sm: The speaker explains how text prediction systems work, starting with Claude Shannon's 1948 pencil and paper experiment that predicted each next word from the previous one and produced only small pockets of coherence. Conditioning on thousands of words gives something like ChatGPT, which can write poetry, lesson plans, code and summaries, but also misinformation. Image diffusion models can generate scenes and realistic models wearing clothing for product catalogs. He then lists limitations. A 2022 UCLA study found models that scored near perfectly on reasoning benchmarks collapsed when problems were presented differently, which he says shows pattern matching rather than deduction. A 2024 study found that adding irrelevant details to math word problems, like the kiwi example, cut performance by up to sixty-five percent. Models retrained repeatedly on their own output degrade, and by the ninth generation one drifted from architecture into rabbits.

The speaker explains the degradation using the data processing inequality, which says processing cannot add information beyond what a signal already contains. Any training set is only a snapshot of what it means to be human, so a model built from it will lose something. He then turns to Hilbert and Russell's push to formalize mathematical proof as symbol manipulation, which made logic a game of syntax divorced from meaning. Kurt Gödel's 1931 incompleteness theorem showed that any system capable of arithmetic contains true statements it cannot prove, so proof and truth are separate things. He argues AI systems are trapped on the syntax side as symbol pushers. Finally, he shows flawed generated images, such as distorted limbs and a person growing out of another's legs, as evidence that diffusion models correlate pixels without understanding human biology.
